newsitem.title: BRAZIL: BRAZIL CONGRESS WEEK-FIGHT LOOMS OVER ELECTION LAW.
newsitem.headline: BRAZIL CONGRESS WEEK-FIGHT LOOMS OVER ELECTION LAW.

text.p: The Brazilian government's uneasy alliance in Congress faced another test this week when a controversial law setting down rules for next year's elections comes up for attention, officials said Monday.

With no votes on major reforms due until next week at the earliest, the only other important piece of legislative action was likely to be a second and final vote in the Chamber of Deputies on a bill extending the government's Fiscal Stabilization Fund (FEF) until 1999.

The Senate was also due to vote on the nomination of Gustavo Franco as the new president of the Central Bank. Franco's nomination was approved last week in a Senate committee and now requires a thumbs-up in a full session of the upper house.
But most eyes were on the electoral bill, which was due to be voted in a Chamber of Deputies committee later this week.
"The fur is going to fly over the electoral law this week. Count on it," said an aide to Deputy Carlos Apolinario, who has penned a initial draft of the legislation.
Brazil goes to the polls in October 1998 to elect a new president, state governors and a sizeable chunk of parliament.
Exactly what candidates can and cannot do during campaigning is traditionally set down in a law which must clear Congress 12 months before the elections.

The task this year has been complicated by the fact that President Fernando Henrique Cardoso and state governors may stand for a second term in 1998 following approval earlier this year of a reform allowing re-election.

The electoral bill has already been stalled for about a month amid inter-party bickering, in particular over proposed restrictions over the use of "the state machine" by candidates seeking re-election.
The government wants to scrap articles that would prevent Cardoso and the governors from inaugurating new roads, dams and other vote-winning public works in the run-up to the elections.

It also wants to halve the election campaign period from a proposed 60 days to a month, relax campaign funding rules, and allow Cardoso to use his presidential jet to attend rallies around Brazil without having to pay for it.

Many of the government's proposed alterations are opposed by allied parties in Congress. Although they are likely to back Cardoso's re-election campaign, they will clash head-on with his friends in many state governorship races.
Congressional officials say if no agreement is forthcoming this week, the bill might be sent straight to the floor of the lower house for a full vote later in August.
